LESSONS.title: Branching with if
LESSONS.goal: Run code only when a condition is true
summary: if condition: runs indented lines if true
== equal, != not equal, < > <= >= size
Indent lines under if by 4 spaces

cards.say: if means “if this is true…”. The indented lines under it run only when the condition is true. The colon (:) at the end of the if line goes with a 4-space indent. Lines that aren't indented always run.
cards.code:
rain = 80
if rain > 60:
    print("Take an umbrella")
print("Off we go!")
cards.out:
Take an umbrella
Off we go!

cards.say: A comparison answers True or False. To ask “are these equal?”, use two equals signs ==. A single = puts a value into a variable, remember? != means not equal, <= means at most, >= means at least.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A comparison is worked out into a single True or False. 1500 is not less than 1200, so it's False.

items.q: It's 15°C. What appears on screen?
items.code:
temp = 15
if temp > 25:
    print("T-shirt")
print("Go out")
items.explain: 15 > 25 is false, so the indented “T-shirt” line is skipped. The unindented “Go out” line runs no matter what the if says.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Perfect!” appears only when the score is exactly 100.
items.explain: To ask “equal?”, use two equals signs ==. You can't put an assignment = in an if condition, so that gives a SyntaxError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.explain: The line under if must be indented 4 spaces. Without it, Python can't tell where the if block is, so it raises IndentationError. The gimbap (Korean rice rolls) will have to wait!

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: "10" in quotes is a string and 10 is a number, so they're different values. That's why it's False. Convert input() values with int() before comparing.

items.q: It's 30°C. Put the lines in order so “Bring water” appears.
items.explain: First set the value, then ask about it with if, then indent what to do when it's true. A variable has to exist before you use it.

items.task: Read a transit card balance with input() and convert it with int() (no prompt text). If the balance is less than 1500, print “Not enough for the bus”, and always print “Check done” at the end. Example: entering 1000 prints two lines, “Not enough for the bus” and “Check done”

tests.expect:
Not enough for the bus
Check done

Not enough for the bus
Check done

hints: With exactly 1500 won you can ride the bus. You're short only when it's less than 1500.
Lines indented under if condition: run only when it's true; unindented lines always run. Think back to the first card.
Under if money < 1500:, indent 4 spaces and print the message. Don't indent “Check done”.

money = int(input())
if money ___ 1500:
    print("___")
print("___")
items.solution:
money = int(input())
if money < 1500:
    print("Not enough for the bus")
print("Check done")
items.explain: Using < means no message at exactly 1500 won. “Check done” isn't indented, so it's outside the if and always runs.

items.q: Which statement about if is true?
options: It runs the indented lines only when the condition is true
You can leave out the colon at the end of the if line
Use a single = to check if two things are equal
items.explain: if runs the indented lines only when the condition is true. The colon at the end is required, and you check equality with ==.

LESSONS.title: Handling the rest with else
LESSONS.goal: Use else to say what to do when the condition is false
summary: else: runs when the if condition is false
Exactly one of if and else runs
else lines up with if and ends with a colon

cards.say: if means “if…”, and else means “otherwise”. Exactly one of the two runs. Let's try a store's 2+1 deal (buy 2, get 1 free)! Write else at the same level as if, with a colon at the end.
You can also split even and odd numbers. If the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0, it's even; otherwise it's odd. Don't write a condition after else. It means “every other case”.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 59 >= 60 is false, so the if part is skipped and the else part runs. Conditions don't give partial credit, not even one point.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Time for bed” appears from 22:00 (10 p.m.) on.
items.code:
time = 23
if time < 22:
    print("Keep studying")
___
    print("Time for bed")
items.explain: else needs a colon at the end of the line, just like if. Without the colon you get a SyntaxError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.explain: Don't write a condition after else. else means “everything the condition above didn't catch”, so it only gets a colon.

items.q: Fill in the blank so 8 counts as even.
items.explain: 8 % 2 is 0. Ask whether the remainder equals 0 with == to go to the even branch.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this?
items.explain: Only one of if and else runs (“Paid”), and the unindented “Receipt printed” always runs. So that's 2 lines.

items.task: Make a ride entry sign. Read a height (cm) with input() and convert it with int() (no prompt text). If it's 120 or more, print “You can ride”; otherwise use else to print “See you next time”. Example: entering 130 prints “You can ride”
hints: Can you ride at exactly 120? “120 or more” includes 120 itself.
if runs when the condition is true, else runs otherwise. “Or more” is written >=.
Under if height >= 120:, print “You can ride”; under else:, print “See you next time”. Indent both.

height = int(input())
if height ___ 120:
    print("___")
___:
    print("___")
items.explain: >= lets someone exactly 120 cm tall ride too. Thanks to else, everyone 119 cm or under gets the message without a separate condition.

items.q: Which statement about if and else is true?
options: Exactly one of if and else runs
You must write a condition after else too
Both if and else can run
items.explain: If the condition is true, the if part runs; if it's false, the else part runs. Only one. else covers everything else, so it has no condition.

LESSONS.title: Many branches with elif
LESSONS.goal: Use elif to split into three or more branches
summary: elif means “or else, if…” and adds a condition
Only the first true branch from the top runs
Put the narrower condition first

cards.say: When you have three or more branches, use elif. It's short for else if. Python checks the conditions one by one from the top, runs only the first true one, and skips the rest.
That's why order matters. 95 also makes >= 80 true, so if that's asked first, Python stops there. We wanted A but got B. Put the narrower condition on top.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 18 >= 28 is false, so we move down to elif. 18 >= 15 is true, so it prints “Cool” and finishes.

items.q: When n is 30, how many lines appear on screen?
items.explain: Both conditions are true, but Python runs the first true one and leaves right away. It never even checks the elif line, so it's 1 line.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Afternoon” appears at 2 p.m.
items.code:
hour = 14
if hour < 12:
    print("Morning")
___ hour < 18:
    print("Afternoon")
else:
    print("Evening")
items.explain: In Python, else if is squeezed into one word: elif. else can't take a condition, so the other two chips give a SyntaxError.

items.q: This person is 70, but “Senior discount” doesn't appear. Why?
options: age >= 20 was true first, so it stopped there
elif is a command that never runs
items.explain: A 70-year-old is also 20 or older, so it stops at the first condition. Moving the 65-or-older check to the top fixes it.

items.q: Fill in the blank so a 70-year-old gets “Senior discount”.
items.explain: Ask the narrower condition, 65 or older, at the very top with >=. Then a 70-year-old gets the senior discount at the first branch.

items.task: Make a fine dust (air pollution) sign. Read the dust level with input() and convert it with int() (no prompt text). Using elif, print “Good” for 30 or less, “Moderate” for 31–80, and “Bad” for 81 or more. Example: entering 31 prints “Moderate”
hints: There are three branches. Look again: which side do the boundaries 30 and 80 belong to?
With if, elif, else, only the first true one from the top runs. “Or less” is <=.
Check Good first with if dust <= 30:, then Moderate with elif dust <= 80:, and the rest is Bad with else.
items.explain: Since Good was already filtered out, elif doesn't need to ask again whether it's 31 or more. Splitting the cases in order from the top with elif keeps it clean.

items.q: Which statement about elif is true?
options: Only the first true branch from the top runs
elif can be used on its own without if
items.explain: In an if/elif/else group, only the first true branch runs. elif can only come after an if.

LESSONS.title: Combining with and/or
LESSONS.goal: Combine conditions with and, or, and not
summary: and: true only when both are true
or: true if either is; not flips it
Write a range at once: 13 <= age < 19
Store a condition's True/False in a variable

cards.say: To check two conditions together, use and and or. and is true only if both are true; or is true if even one is. Let's look at a store discount: the total is high enough, but there aren't enough stamps.
cards.code:
price = 12000
stamp = 3
print(price >= 10000 and stamp >= 5)
print(price >= 10000 or stamp >= 5)

cards.say: not flips true and false. You can write a range in one go, like 13 <= age < 19, just like in math class. Nice, right? It means 13 or more and under 19.
cards.code:
age = 15
if 13 <= age < 19:
    print("Teen")
print(not age > 20)

cards.say: A condition is a calculation too, so its result is True or False. Store it in a variable and you can just write the name after if. It's like putting a name tag on a long condition.
cards.code:
kor = 70
math = 55
ok = kor >= 60 and math >= 60
print(ok)
if ok:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Retake")

items.q: What's the output?
items.code: print(3 > 1 and 2 > 5)
items.explain: 3 > 1 is true, but 2 > 5 is false. With and, if even one is false, the result is False.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: or is true if even one of the two is true. day == "Sat" is true, so it's the weekend fare.

items.q: Fill in the blank so you can ride only if you're 120 cm or taller and 7 or older.
items.explain: “120 cm or taller and 7 or older” means both must be true, so it's and. With or, a tall 6-year-old would get on.

items.q: Fill in the blank so only scores from 0 to 100 are valid.
items.explain: 100 must be included, so it's <= (or less). The symbols always go < then =; =< is a SyntaxError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get if you enter 20?
items.explain: input() always gives you a string. The string "20" and the number 19 can't be compared by size, so it's a TypeError. int(input()) fixes it.

items.q: Put the lines in order so “Careful outside” appears when it's too hot or too cold.
items.explain: 33°C is above 30, so the first condition of or is true. It runs if even one of the two is true.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Pass” appears if either score is 60 or more.
items.code:
a = 80
b = 50
ok = a >= 60 or b >= 60
if ___:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")
items.explain: ok already holds True, so its name alone works as a condition. not ok flips it to Fail, and ok() calls a value like a function, which is a TypeError.

items.task: It's a convenience store checkout. Read the amount on the first line and membership (Y or N) on the second with input() (no prompt text). Join the two conditions with and: for a member spending 10000 won or more, print amount * 9 // 10; otherwise print the amount as is. Example: 12000 and Y → 10800
hints: There are two discount conditions: is it a member, and is it 10000 won or more? Exactly 10000 won gets the discount too.
and was true only when both conditions are true. Check whether strings are equal like member == "Y".
On one if line, join the amount condition and the member condition with and. If true, print the discounted amount; under else, print amount.
items.explain: Joining the two with and sends non-members and small amounts to else. Converting the amount with int() and comparing membership as a string is exactly right.

items.q: Which statement about and and or is true?
options: and is true only when both conditions are true
or is true only when both conditions are true
not joins two conditions into one
items.explain: and needs both to be true; or is true if even one is. not flips the true/false of a single condition.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 3 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Split cases with if/elif/else, comparisons and logic
summary: == compares, = assigns
Only the first true branch runs; order matters
Join with and/or; indent 4 spaces

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 3. Here we pick what to bring based on the rain and wind. First guess which branch will run, then check the result. If you got it, you're ready!

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
a = 3
b = a == 4
print(b)
items.explain: In b = a == 4, the == comparison happens first and gives False, then = puts that value into b. The number of equals signs changes what they do.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
n = 3
if n > 0:
    print("Positive")
  print("End")
items.explain: The last line has 2 spaces, so it's neither inside nor outside the if. Use 4 spaces for inside or 0 for outside and the clue goes away.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Top up needed” appears when the transit card balance is too low.
items.code:
money = 800
if money >= 1500:
    print("Get on")
___
    print("Top up needed")
items.explain: Every other case is caught by else: with no condition. elif must have a condition, and else must have a colon.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 90 >= 90 is true. “Or more” includes the number itself, so it prints A at the first branch and finishes.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Day off” appears on a Sunday or a holiday.
items.explain: “Or” means one true condition is enough, so it's or. With and, you'd only get a day off on a Sunday that's also a holiday.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The string "10" and the number 10 are different, so False. Converting with int() makes them equal, so True.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: money >= 1500 is false, and not flips it to true. So the if part, “Top up needed”, appears.

items.q: The height is 110 cm. Put the lines in order so “See you next time” appears.
items.explain: Right under if goes what to do when it's true; under else, what to do in every other case. Indent both. 110 is less than 120, so it's the else part.

items.task: Make a fare sign for the Ria Village Bus. Read an age with input() and convert it with int() (no prompt text). Print “Child 500 won” for 12 or under, “Teen 900 won” for 13–18, and “Adult 1500 won” for 19 or over. Example: entering 13 prints “Teen 900 won”
hints: Check the boundary ages again: 12 is a child, 13 and 18 are teens, 19 is an adult.
Three branches meant if, elif, else. Only the first true one from the top runs.
Filter children first with if age <= 12:. Next, elif age <= 18: is for teens, and else catches adults.
items.explain: Since children were filtered first, elif only needs to ask “18 or under?” for teens. It's right at every boundary: 12, 13, 18 and 19.

items.q: Which statement about Chapter 3 is true?
options: In if/elif/else, only the first true branch runs
Use = to check equality in an if condition
Lines under if don't need to be indented
input() values can be compared with numbers right away
items.explain: Only the first true branch runs. Check equality with ==, indent 4 spaces under if, and convert input() values with int() before comparing.

ADVANCED.title: Merging conditions
ADVANCED.goal: Merge conditions into one line and pick values with a conditional expression
summary: Merge nested ifs into one line with and
Pick in one go: a if condition else b
Store a condition's result (True/False) too

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Remember and from 3-4? Putting an if inside an if gets long, so let's join them with and into one line.
To pick one value, a conditional expression is handy. The order is: value-if-true if condition else value-if-false. It reads almost like an English sentence. You can store the result in a variable.
cards.code:
n = 7
word = "big" if n > 5 else "small"
print(word)

items.q: if x < 10: is nested inside if x > 0:. How do you write it in one line?
items.explain: Both conditions are needed, so it's and. or passes if just one matches, which changes the meaning of the nested ifs. A comma is a SyntaxError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
x = 5
print("big" if x > 3 else "small")
items.explain: x > 3 is true, so the value in front, “big”, is picked. If the condition were false, the value after else would come out.

items.q: Fill in the blank so 7 prints “odd”.
items.code:
n = 7
w = "odd" if n % 2 ___ 1 else "even"
print(w)
items.explain: 7 % 2 is 1. Asking whether the remainder equals 1 with == picks the value in front, “odd”.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
s = 75
print(60 <= s < 80 and s != 70)
items.explain: 60 <= 75 < 80 is true, and 75 != 70 is true too. Both sides of and are true, so it's True.

items.q: It's 5°C. Put the lines in order so “cold” appears.
items.explain: Make the value, pick msg with a conditional expression, then print it at the end. A variable has to exist before you use it.

items.task: Read a Korean language score and a math score, one per line, with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and convert them with int(). Check with and whether both are 60 or more and store it in ok, then use a conditional expression to pick “Pass” or “Retake”, store it in result, and print it. Example: 70 and 80 → Pass
hints: Pass means both subjects are 60 or more. Exactly 60 passes too.
and is true only when both conditions are true. The conditional expression for picking a value is the “value if condition else value” from the card.
First join the two score checks with and and store the result in ok. Then pick with result = value if ok else value, and print it.

kor = int(input())
mat = int(input())
ok = kor >= 60 ___ mat >= 60
result = "___" if ok else "___"
print(result)
items.solution:
kor = int(input())
mat = int(input())
ok = kor >= 60 and mat >= 60
result = "Pass" if ok else "Retake"
print(result)
items.explain: and checks both subjects at once, and the conditional expression picks the word. Even one subject at 59 means a retake: that's the power of and.

items.q: Which statement about the conditional expression “A if condition else B” is true?
options: If the condition is true A is picked; if false, B
If the condition is true B is picked; if false, A
items.explain: The value before the condition is the one for true. Only one is picked, and you can store it in a variable or print it right away.

ADVANCED.title: Splitting with match
ADVANCED.goal: Branch on a value using match and case
summary: match value: find the matching case below
Join several values with |, like case 1 | 2:
case _: catches everything else (goes last)

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. If you keep checking the same value with ==, match is neater. The case that matches runs, and | joins several values.
cards.code:
day = "Sat"
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        print("Weekend")
    case _:
        print("Weekday")

cards.say: Numbers work the same way. case _: catches everything else, like else. Only the first matching case from the top runs, and _ matches any value, so put it last; a case below it is a SyntaxError.
cards.code:
grade = 2
match grade:
    case 1:
        print("Freshman")
    case 2 | 3:
        print("Middle")
    case _:
        print("Other")

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
size = "L"
match size:
    case "S":
        print("Small cup")
    case "M":
        print("Medium cup")
    case _:
        print("Large cup")
items.explain: “L” is neither S nor M, so it reaches the last case _:. _ catches the rest when nothing above matched.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
num = 9
match num:
    case 1:
        print("One")
    case 2:
        print("Two")
print("End")
items.explain: With no matching case and no case _:, match does nothing and moves on. The unindented “End” always runs.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Stop” appears when cmd is s or q.
items.code:
cmd = "q"
match cmd:
    case "s" ___ "q":
        print("Stop")
    case _:
        print("Keep going")
items.explain: To join several values in a case, use the vertical bar |. Neither or nor and can go in a case, so both give a SyntaxError.

items.q: Fill in the blank so every light except red gets “Go”.
items.code:
light = "green"
match light:
    case "red":
        print("Stop")
    ___
        print("Go")
items.explain: In match, the rest is caught by case _:, not else. else can't be used inside match.

items.q: It's Sunday. Put the lines in order so “Weekend” appears.
items.explain: Indent case under match, then indent once more under case for what to do. case _: goes last.

items.task: Show what a cafe order code means. Read one letter with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Using match, print “Americano” for A, “Latte” for B or C, and “Not on the menu” for anything else. Example: entering B prints “Latte”
hints: There are three branches: A, B and C, and the rest. Compare the input letter as it is.
Under match value:, list the cases one after another, join several values with |, and catch the rest with case _:.
Under match code:, indent case "A":, case "B" | "C":, and case _: in order, and print in each.

code = input()
match code:
    case "A":
        print("___")
    case "B" ___ "C":
        print("___")
    case ___:
        print("___")
items.solution:
code = input()
match code:
    case "A":
        print("Americano")
    case "B" | "C":
        print("Latte")
    case _:
        print("Not on the menu")
items.explain: | joins B and C into one branch, and case _: makes sure any letter gets a message. Splitting the cases with match keeps it clean.

items.q: Which statement about match is true?
options: Only the first matching case from the top runs
case _: must go at the top
items.explain: Like if/elif, only the first matching case runs. _ matches every value, so if any case comes after case _:, Python refuses to run the code and raises a SyntaxError. That's why case _: always goes last.

ADVANCED.title: Practice: fare table
ADVANCED.goal: Calculate a fare using match and a conditional expression
summary: Set the base fare with match
Apply the discount with or and a conditional expression
Check the boundary ages (12/13, 64/65)

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. Let's build an amusement park fare table. First, use match to store a base fare in a variable based on the day.
cards.code:
day = "Fri"
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        fee = 5000
    case _:
        fee = 3000
print(fee)

cards.say: Next, the discount. Kids and seniors pay half; everyone else pays full price. Join the two age conditions with or and pick the value with a conditional expression. Put the two together and the fare table is done.
cards.code:
age = 8
fee = 4000
ok = age <= 12 or age >= 65
print(fee // 2 if ok else fee)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
day = "Sun"
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        fee = 5000
    case _:
        fee = 3000
print(fee)
items.explain: “Sun” matches case "Sat" | "Sun":. fee is set to 5000, and case _: doesn't run.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
age = 70
fee = 4000
ok = age <= 12 or age >= 65
print(fee // 2 if ok else fee)
items.explain: 70 is 65 or more, so the second condition of or is true. That picks the half price fee // 2, so 2000 is printed.

items.q: Fill in the blank so Saturday costs 5000.
items.code:
day = "Sat"
match day:
    case "Sat" ___ "Sun":
        fee = 5000
    case _:
        fee = 3000
print(fee)
items.explain: Joining the two weekend days into one branch takes |. Both or and + give a SyntaxError in a case.

items.q: Fill in the blank so a 70-year-old pays half.
items.code:
age = 70
fee = 4000
if age <= 12 ___ age >= 65:
    fee = fee // 2
print(fee)
items.explain: Kids or seniors get the discount, so it's or. With and, no age is both 12 or under and 65 or over, so nobody would get a discount.

items.q: The visitor is 70. Put the lines in order so 2000 appears.
items.explain: Make age → store the discount condition joined with or in ok → pick fee with a conditional expression and print it. Names must exist before you use them.

items.task: Amusement park tickets! Read the day (like Sat) and the age, one per line, with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Use match to set fee: 5000 for Sat/Sun, 4000 for Fri, 3000 otherwise. Put “12 or under or 65 or over” (joined with or) in disc. Then use a conditional expression to put half price (fee // 2) or fee into price, and print “Fare” and price. Example: Sat, 30 → Fare 5000
hints: The day sets the base fare, and the age sets the discount. 12 gets the discount, 13 doesn't, and 65 does.
The day went into fee with match, and the age used a condition joined with or plus “value if condition else value”.
Under match day:, put case "Sat" | "Sun":, case "Fri":, case _: and set fee. For the age, join with or into disc and pick price with a conditional expression.

match day:
    case "Sat" ___ "Sun":
        fee = 5000
    case "Fri":
        fee = ___
    case _:
        fee = 3000
disc = age <= 12 ___ age ___ 65
price = fee // 2 if disc else fee
print("Fare", price)
items.solution:
day = input()
age = int(input())
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        fee = 5000
    case "Fri":
        fee = 4000
    case _:
        fee = 3000
disc = age <= 12 or age >= 65
price = fee // 2 if disc else fee
print("Fare", price)
items.explain: match handles the base fare, while or and a conditional expression handle the discount. It's right at the 12/13 and 64/65 boundaries too.

items.q: Which statement about the fare table code is true?
options: match splits the days; or and a conditional expression handle the discount
All the age comparisons must also happen inside match
With or, both conditions must be true for a discount
items.explain: Days with fixed values go to match, and ages compared by size go to conditions, which reads easily. or is true if even one side is true.

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so “You win!” appears when your pick matches the lucky number.
TEMPLATES.explain: To ask “equal?”, use two equals signs ==. = is assignment, so in an if condition it's a SyntaxError. != means not equal, so you'd get “No luck”.

TEMPLATES.q: The temperature equals the limit exactly. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: {T} >= {T} is true (“or more” includes the same value). > doesn't include the same value. And if the line under if isn't indented, it's an IndentationError.

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so a long trip shows only “Long way”, and other trips check the next condition.
TEMPLATES.explain: elif is checked only when the condition above is false. A plain if starts a new if statement, so “Medium way” would print too, and else can't take a condition, so it's a SyntaxError.
